newsitem.title: USA: Dollar dips, steadies after small Fed rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Dollar dips, steadies after small Fed rate hike.

text.p: A broadly expected interest rate hike by Federal Reserve policymakers left the dollar rattled but ultimately little changed on Tuesday, and the prospect of further monetary tightening will keep a modest bid under the currency in coming weeks, traders and analysts said.
The prospect of tighter U.S. credit could put pressure on domestic stock and bond prices, which would likely stunt any dollar rally, experts added.

"A rise in U.S. rates depresses asset values in the United States. If we see substantial capital losses, that could work against the (benefit of) higher interest rates," said Tim McGee, international economist at Tokai Bank.

The Fed's policymaking Federal Open Market Committee ended its regular meeting on Tuesday with an announcement that it had boosted its overnight federal funds lending rate target to 5.50 percent from 5.25.
The dollar immediately fell half a pfennig to below 1.69 marks, then spiked higher before settling near pre-announcement levels.z
The Dow industrials initially firmed but then fell modestly, mimicking the reaction in the 30-year Treasury bond.
Analysts said the Fed action will have conflicting impacts on the dollar, with the economic restraint of higher rates offsetting an inflation-fighting boost for the dollar.
"I don't think we're going to see too much, but if anything, the dollar will be slightly bid," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc.
"People have been looking for something to do with the dollar and this rate move may do it, particulary if the bond market doesn't react too badly," he added.
The Fed last shifted interest rates on January 31, 1996, when it cut the fed funds rate to 5.25 percent from 5.50 percent and the discount rate to 5.0 percent from 5.25.
The Fed's last rate hike occurred on February 1, 1995, when it lifted the funds rate to 6.0 percent from 5.50 and the discount rate to 5.25 percent from 4.75.
The likelihood that the already attractive gap between U.S. fixed-income rates and their foreign counterparts will widen even further offers an implicitly dollar-bullish argument, analysts said.
With Japan and continental Europe still suffering from anemic economic growth, interest rates are likely to stay low abroad, highlighting the appeal of meatier U.S. yields.
"When you look overseas, (policymakers) are not going to follow the Fed (rate hike) and because of that, the dollar will eventually move higher," Iggo said.

Analysts must now attempt to determine the timing of the next Fed move. Many economists expect more rate hikes later this year, which could further balloon the yield spread between U.S. and foreign bonds.
"We think ultimately that will lead to a stronger dollar, but today, we're trading off the back of the asset markets," said Iggo. "Hysteria has taken over a bit."

Further rate hikes would primarily boost the dollar against the weakest currencies in Europe, not necessarily the mark, said Mark Gargano, manager of currency derivatives at First Union National Bank.
"You buy dollar/Spain, dollar/lira, dollar/Sweden, more vulnerable currencies," Gargano said.
But aggressive tightening could deflate U.S. stock and bond markets and put the brakes on the U.S. economy, which would hamper the dollar, analysts said.
"More aggressive rate hikes are more likely to move you into a period of falling rates sooner because the economy is likely to be slowing down," McGee said.
